name: Karl Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a construction crew for the power company, building new lines out to solar and wind farms. Where I live it's flat farmland as far as you can see, and every year another field turns into solar panels that need connecting. So a normal day is setting new poles with the digger truck, framing them, pulling in conductor and making the final connections at the substation. I like building something new that'll still be standing when my kids are grown. What I don't like is the mud in spring and the delays when the paperwork isn't ready.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does being crew lead mean for you day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I plan the work, keep everyone safe and talk to the engineers and the landowners. I'm the one the farmer yells at when we drive over his wheat, and the one who calms him down. I've done this nineteen years and I'm good at reading drawings and spotting mistakes before they cost us. Our region's on a lower pay grade than the coast, and there's no other line work for a long way, so we're careful with money. My wife, Inês, works part-time at the pharmacy in town, and with two teenagers and the mortgage, we've rarely got more than a few weeks put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, that's what I expected. The tools help a bit with emails and that's about it. We'd all have a laugh about the people who said it would change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine with it. My work's steady because of all the solar and wind, and AI going nowhere doesn't change that. I use the chat tool now and then to write a polite email to an angry landowner, and that's useful, but I wouldn't miss it terribly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job. Maybe use the AI tools a bit more for the paperwork, since I'd seen the engineers using them without trouble. And I'd keep trying to put a bit aside each month, which is hard enough as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty normal, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the email to the angry landowner.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a farmer called Mr. Hale who's been fighting the new line across his land for a year. I'm not good with words when I'm annoyed, so I typed in what I wanted to say, rude version, and asked it to make it polite. It came out sounding like a lawyer, so I changed it back a bit. He actually replied nicely, first time ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said putting a bit aside is hard enough. What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teenagers, mainly. Leo's fifteen and eats like a horse, and Bia needs something new every term. Then the car needs tyres, or the boiler needs a part. We try for fifty a week into savings, and some weeks it happens and some weeks it doesn't.

S0.say: I'd say that's what I expected, since the tools help a bit with emails and not much else. We'd all laugh about the people who said it would change everything.
S0.think: I'd be fine, because my work is steady thanks to solar and wind building. I use the chat tool now and then for polite emails to angry landowners, but I wouldn't miss it much.
S0.do: Carries on with his job and uses AI tools a bit more for paperwork once he's seen engineers use them without trouble. Keeps trying to save about fifty a week.
S0.quote: I typed in what I wanted to say, rude version, and asked it to make it polite.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is practical and even-tempered, and his work is steady thanks to renewable energy projects. He uses AI tools occasionally and finds them mildly useful. Saving is a constant struggle because of teenagers and household repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but people adapt. Some jobs go, new ones come. I'd tell my crew to learn what they need to learn and not get too worked up about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's actually okay, maybe even good. All this AI needs power, and power needs lines, and my crew builds lines. If anything, we'd be busier. The office side might shrink, the planners and the people who do the permits, but not us, not for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the training on whatever new tools the company brings in, once a couple of other crews had tried them. I'd try to grab overtime while the building boom lasts and put it toward savings and the mortgage. Maybe I'd help Inês look at courses, because I'd worry the pharmacy might use more machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little worried for Inês.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the worry for Inês?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pharmacy's already got a machine that counts pills. If it gets smarter, maybe they need fewer people at the counter. She's good with the old folks, they ask for her by name, but I'm not sure the owner thinks about that when he's looking at costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell your crew not to get worked up. Who on the crew might struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamal, my best digger operator, he's fifty-six and hates anything with a screen. If the new digger trucks come with fancy controls, he'd struggle. I'd pair him with one of the young lads, let them teach each other, the lad learns the old tricks, Jamal learns the screen.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big change but people adapt, as some jobs go and new ones come. I'd tell my crew to learn what they need and not get too worked up.
S1.think: For me it's okay, maybe good, because AI needs power and power needs lines, so my crew would be busier. The office side might shrink, but not us for a while.
S1.do: Takes training on new company tools once other crews have tried them and grabs overtime during the building boom to put towards savings and the mortgage. Helps his wife look at courses in case the pharmacy automates.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a little worry for his wife.
S1.quote: All this AI needs power, and power needs lines, and my crew builds lines.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as potentially good for his crew, since it would boost line construction. His concern is for his wife's job and for Jamal, an older operator. His pairing idea shows a practical, team-minded approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and everybody needs to work together, government and companies, to get through it. I'd try not to panic people, but I'd be honest that it's serious. You can't pretend that away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried sick. If robots can build lines by 2028, my job's gone, and Inês's probably too. Few weeks of savings, a mortgage, two teenagers, and nothing else here. Two years isn't enough time to do anything except brace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything we could straight away, no holidays, no new phones, cheaper food. I'd try to pick up weekend electrical jobs for neighbours, fixing wiring and the like, for as long as people still wanted a person. And we'd talk to Inês's parents about help, they've got a bit put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Lying awake thinking about the mortgage letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the mortgage letter'. What do you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one that says you're behind. I've seen it once, years ago, when I had a back injury and was off three months. That letter's on the kitchen table, white envelope, red print. I never want to see it again, and in this picture I'd be expecting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel asking Inês's parents for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward. Her dad never thought I earned enough. But they'd help, for the kids. I'd tell myself it's a loan and pay it back. Pride's a luxury when you're short.

S2.say: I'd say it's a huge shock and government and companies need to work together. I'd try not to panic people, but I'd be honest that it's serious.
S2.think: Privately I'd be worried sick, since robots building lines by 2028 would take my job and likely my wife's. With a few weeks of savings and nothing else here, two years is only enough time to brace.
S2.do: Cuts holidays, new phones and food costs right away and picks up weekend electrical jobs for neighbours while people still want a person. Talks to his wife's parents about financial help.
S2.feel: Scared, lying awake thinking about the mortgage letter.
S2.quote: That letter's on the kitchen table, white envelope, red print.
S2.fieldNote: His calm public tone hides real fear about losing both incomes. A past mortgage arrears letter during a back injury is a vivid memory that shapes his fear. He'd swallow his pride to ask his in-laws for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable if we start now. I'd tell the crew to think about savings and skills. I'd say the government should start planning now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps a lot. Leo would be through school and Bia nearly. I could save a bit more and maybe build up the side work. But I don't see a long-term job for me after that, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting every bit of overtime into savings and try to clear the car loan. I'd get the electrician's licence for house wiring, so I could do side jobs properly, maybe in year one or two. And once a few people I trust were using the AI tools for planning and quotes, I'd learn those too, so I could run a small side business more easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the side business something you've thought about before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Neighbours always ask me to look at their wiring, and I usually do it for a beer. My cousin Rui does house wiring in the next town and he's always busy. With five years I could build it up slowly, see if it could keep us going for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't see a long-term job after that. How do you sit with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well. I'm the type who likes a plan, and this one stops at year five. But maybe by then there's something new, or some government plan. I'd just try to keep us afloat and see.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but workable if we start now, and tell the crew to think about savings and skills. I'd say the government should plan now, not in year four.
S3.think: Five years helps a lot, since one child would be through school and the other nearly. But I don't see a long-term job for me after that.
S3.do: Puts all overtime into savings, clears the car loan, and gets a house-wiring licence in the first two years for proper side jobs. Learns AI tools for planning and quotes once people he trusts use them, to run a small side business.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: I'm the type who likes a plan, and this one stops at year five.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him build a side business in house wiring, with his cousin as a model. He's open to AI tools once trusted people use them. He admits the plan has an end date and doesn't know what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning, and we've got no excuse not to be ready. I'd tell people to plan sensibly, save and learn new skills. I'd probably say the government should help, but people should do their part too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes a big difference. Kids grown and gone, mortgage smaller, and I'd be fifty-three. Maybe I'd have time to move into something else, or build the side work up properly. It's not great, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save steadily, pay extra on the mortgage, and get the house-wiring licence early on. I'd watch for retraining options and take one once it was clear which jobs were holding up. And I'd talk with Leo and Bia about their studies, pushing them toward things that keep options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly okay. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo about his own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to be a mechanic, like his uncle. I'd tell him to go for it but learn the electric and computer side of cars too. Keep an eye on what's changing, don't get stuck. That's what I wish someone had told me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what's the biggest change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to breathe. With two years, it's panic and cutting back. With ten, I can plan, save, let the kids grow up first. It's the difference between being hit by a truck and seeing it coming down the road.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning and there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd tell people to save and learn new skills, with government helping but people doing their part too.
S4.think: Ten years makes a big difference, with the kids grown, a smaller mortgage and me at fifty-three. I might move into something else or build up side work, so I can see a path.
S4.do: Saves steadily, pays extra on the mortgage and gets the house-wiring licence early. Takes a retraining option once it's clear which jobs are holding up, and steers his children towards studies that keep options open.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy but mostly okay, because it feels manageable.
S4.quote: It's the difference between being hit by a truck and seeing it coming down the road.
S4.fieldNote: The decade gives him room to plan, with the children grown before the change arrives. He'd retrain only once it was clear which jobs last, which fits his steady nature. He balances a call for government help with personal responsibility.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. We'd lose both our jobs with a few weeks' savings and no time to prepare. What would help is some kind of bridge, money to cover the mortgage for a year or two, and cheap training so I could learn something new without going broke.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are proud of. I'm proud of the lines I've built. You can drive past a solar farm and say, 'I connected that.' A robot might do it better someday, but I'd miss having something to point at.

headlineQuote: You can drive past a solar farm and say, 'I connected that.'
portrait: Karl Costa is a 43-year-old crew lead building new power lines to solar and wind farms across flat farmland, with a wife who works part-time at a pharmacy, two teenagers and a mortgage. He's skilled and respected but paid on a lower regional grade, and the family rarely has more than a few weeks saved. He uses AI tools now and then and adopts new things once he's seen others make them work. He's calm if AI plateaus or changes things steadily, since the grid build-out keeps his crew busy, but alarmed by two-year AGI. With five years he'd build a house-wiring side business, and with ten he sees a manageable path once his kids are grown.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he and his wife would lose both jobs with only a few weeks of savings and no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge to cover the mortgage for a year or two and cheap training so he could learn something new without going broke.
